# FLAGS
map and retext: --verbatim; 
undo: --entry; 
sync: --for;
watch: --once, 
ack: the number of the writing
tip: --add <new line> --after <words of a line in the entry>, saves the new line in the entry under that line and the tip asks to compile it; on a file with no abstraction, --add saves the new line as its first entry;


# COMMANDS

[human init](cmd_init):
    creates the human folder in the project.
    create human/human.json with the list of the project's files.
    
    if none yet, human/human.json gets a short random name as an id
    prints the id and the count of files.
    
    [sweep](scan_files) the project folder and its code files
    drop hidden files, 
    build folders, 
    if folders with a map of their own then pass through [the sieve](is_ignored)
    fill the ignore list of human.json
    add human files to human.json, each with the folder it shows in
    
    a map with the old name explanation_ gets the new name abstraction_, and an old human/project.json with words becomes a human file named after the project folder.
    if the project has no human file yet, make the first human file, named after the project folder, and print its name.
    for each file that is not on disk: delete the its map in human/
    
    if a file at the top of the folder answers to the bare name of a human file:
        show warning that the file needs a new path to be told apart.

    [runs human serve](serve_away)

    

[human serve](cmd_serve):
    finds the top of the project
    if server already runs, [give the server the project](hand_over), [print the reader's link](print_links), stop
    else: 
        start a server in port 8010 unless you say --port <number>
        if new project, create .human in /human/ with project id, [create project id in ~/.human/projects.json](add_project)
    
    [read the list of projects](read_projects) in ~/.human/projects.json. 
    [find project](project_root) by: /<project id>/ 
    
    print:
        "Click <localhost address> to read your human code!"
        if machine has tailnet and is not Windows, print "This is the tailnet <[tailnet address](tailnet_ip)> in case you need it : )", 
    
    [the server running on port <number>](FreshHandler), serves:
        /<project>/..., a file of that project as it is on disk
        /<project>/human/web.html [from ~/.human/web.html](deploy_reader)
        /human/human.json, [rebuilt](fresh_map) on every request, with [the time each map last changed](map_stamps)
        /human/server/queue, the updates that are not worked yet by the ai harness.
    
    the server takes [as JSON](read_body):
        1. a writing from the reader             — your own words on an entry, a first
                                              telling for a file with no map, or the
                                              code of that file; the desk hands it to
                                              [the queue](compiler/cli/human/cmd_watch.py:save_writing),
                                              which runs the command you would have
                                              typed and keeps the writing saved.
                                              When you compile the file, the desk
                                              sends its saved writings to claude.
                                              When the writing grows a few words of an
                                              entry, the desk passes those marked words
                                              along with it, so the queue knows which
                                              part to grow
        2. a new file from the reader            ([the new file](new_file)) — you name a
                                              path from the top of the project; the
                                              desk makes the file there, empty, and
                                              puts it in the list of the book, so it
                                              waits for its telling. A path that leaves
                                              the project, goes into the human folder,
                                              a hidden or build folder, or a project of
                                              its own, a name with a dot in front, a
                                              suffix the list does not know, a path the
                                              ignore list drops, or a file that is
                                              already there is refused, with the reason

        3. if a new human file from the reader:
            one bare word, no folder and no suffix,
            [the folder](human_place) you made it in, which the map keeps as its place; 
            the desk opens an empty map under that name, for words that stand on no code. 
            a name with a folder, a suffix or a dot in front, 
            a name another human file holds, or a name a file at the root holds is refused, with the reason. 
            a folder is dropped if it leaves the project to go to:
            the human folder, 
            a hidden or build folder, 
            or not on disk
            the map stands at the top

        4. Any other writing gets "not found". Every answer
            carries "do not keep me" ([the note](end_headers)), so a
            reload never shows an old copy, and the desk stays quiet
            unless you add --log ([the mute](log_message)).
            A save the desk refuses still prints a line with the time,
            the file, the entry and the reason.

[human map file --verbatim](compiler/cli/human/cmd_map.py)
  an abstraction the user sends.
  if --verbatim yes, mark as verbatim.
  the name is a file or a human file by its bare name.
  a folder is refused: a folder has no map.
  the desk hands the whole line to the map run
  [the guard](compiler/cli/human/cmd_map.py) there keeps the words as you wrote them — they go in plain. 
  a pin in the abstraction is refused.

human retext, undo, show, lines, sync <file>       ([the engine](compiler/cli/human/compiler.py))
    All the work on a map that exists. The desk only points
    the way. retext takes --verbatim too, to put words of your
    own in the place of the ones already mapped. undo takes
    --entry, the number of the entry to drop; without it the
    last entry written goes. sync takes --for, the number of
    the entry the code change was written for: that entry keeps
    its words and only its spans and pins follow. A stale
    repair takes no --for.
    A folder in the place of the file is refused.

human retext, undo, show, lines, sync <human file> ([the project hand](compiler/cli/human/cmd_human.py))
    The same commands with the bare name of a human file where
    the file goes: the desk sends them to the hand that works on
    the maps of human files, before the engine sees them.

[human watch / human ack <number>](compiler/cli/human/cmd_watch.py)
    print every abstraction event ai harness has not compiled, one line each
    each event stays at a queue for the next print; 
    if --once, print and returns.
    if ack <number>, 
        mark the abstraction as compiled and says
        show many abstraction still wait for compilation

[human skills](cmd_skills)
    copy the skill folders, 
    save to ai harnesses skill folders

[human update](cmd_update)
    works only on the built human program, else stop
    read the newest version, download it and put the skills of that version in place
    if no newer version, print that this human is the newest
    else print the new version is installed

[human uninstall](cmd_uninstall)
    works only on the built human program, else stop
    delete the human skill folders from the ai harnesses skill folders
    delete ~/.human and the human command, then print that human is uninstalled

anchors.words: the time each map last changed

explanations.text:
●  you open the door                                    ([the shelf](cmd_serve))
  │     You type: human serve.
  │     The tool climbs to the top of the project — the folder
  │     that holds human/ — so the command works from any
  │     folder inside the project.
  │     It reads the id of the project in human/human.json. A
  │     project with no id stops here, with the reason.
  │     Then it knocks on door 8010 of your machine. When a
  │     human server already stands there, the tool gives it
  │     this project, prints the addresses, and ends: one
  │     server reads all your projects. When that server
  │     refuses the project, the tool stops with its reason.
  │     When no server answers, all that the tool prints from
  │     now on goes to your screen and also into
  │     human/server/serve.log, so you can read it later. When
  │     human init started the server, the print already goes
  │     to that log, and the tool does not write it two times.
  │     When no server answers, the tool writes the project
  │     into the list of projects in its own folder, ~/.human,
  │     brings the old maps of this project up to date,
  │     copies the reader there when the copy is old or not
  │     there, takes door 8010 and stands there. On Windows the
  │     door opens only to this machine; on other machines it
  │     opens to other machines too, such as your tailnet.
  │     When another program, or a human server older than
  │     this one, holds the door, the tool stops and tells you
  │     so.
  │     It prints the addresses to read at; each address
  │     carries the id of the project.
  │     While it stands, it looks for a newer human once each
  │     hour and gets it ready, when it runs as a downloaded
  │     program.
  │
  ●  the browser knocks                             ([the fresh copy](FreshHandler))
  │     You open http://localhost:8010/<id>/human/web.html.
  │     Each thing on the page — the reader, the maps, the code —
  │     is one knock: "give me this file".
  │     The knocks of one page go on one line that the tool keeps
  │     open, and it closes a line that stays quiet for 30
  │     seconds.
  │     The [first part of each knock](project) names the
  │     project by its id. The tool finds the project in its
  │     list; a knock for an id it does not know, or for a
  │     project with no human/human.json, gets "no project".
  │     When the tool takes a project, and when it starts with
  │     a project, the tool brings the old maps of that project
  │     up to date: a map
  │     with the old name explanation_ gets the new name
  │     abstraction_, and an old project map with words becomes
  │     a human file named after the project folder.
  │     A knock for the bare id goes on to the reader.
  │     The reader itself comes from the tool's own folder, the
  │     same for every project.
  │     The tool hands out only files under the top of the
  │     project, never anything above it.
  │     The page can also ask for all the maps in one knock: the
  │     map of each file that is still on disk and each human
  │     file. A map that is not good JSON is left out.
  │     A knock for /human/hello, with no project, gets the
  │     version of the tool, so a new serve knows a human
  │     server stands at the door.
  │
  ●  the reader sends a writing back
  │     In the reader you can write yourself: new words for an
  │     entry, a first telling for a file with no map, or the
  │     code of that file. The writing comes back as its own
  │     knock and the tool writes it into the map or the file at
  │     once and keeps it as saved. When you compile the file,
  │     its saved writings go into the queue in human/server/,
  │     where the agent takes them with human watch. When you mark
  │     a few words of an entry to grow them, those words go with
  │     the writing, so the agent knows which part to grow.
  │     The page can also ask for that queue and see what still
  │     waits.
  │
  ●  the reader asks for a new file                  ([the new file](new_file))
  │     In the reader you can name a path from the top of the
  │     project. The tool makes the file there, empty, and puts
  │     it in the list of files in human/human.json, so it waits
  │     for its telling. It refuses, with the reason, a path that
  │     leaves the project, goes into the human folder, a hidden
  │     or build folder, or a project of its own, a name with a
  │     dot in front, a suffix the file tree does not know, a
  │     path the ignore list drops, or a file that is already
  │     there.
  │
  ●  the reader asks for a new human file            ([the human file](new_human))
  │     In the reader you can also ask for words that stand on
  │     no code. You give one bare word — no folder, no suffix —
  │     and the tool opens an empty map under that name, ready
  │     for its abstraction, with no file under it. It refuses,
  │     with the reason, a name that carries a folder, a suffix
  │     or a dot in front, a name another human file already
  │     holds, or a name a file at the root holds.
  │     With the name you can send [a folder](human_place) of the
  │     project to keep the map beside. The tool writes that
  │     folder into the map, so the reader shows the map there
  │     and the word back names it as that folder over the name.
  │     A folder that leaves the project, one in the human folder
  │     or in a hidden or build folder, and one that is not on
  │     disk, is dropped: the map stands at the top instead.
  │     A knock that is not a writing, a compile, a new file, or a new
  │     human file gets "not found".
  │
  ●  every answer says: do not keep me                    ([the note](end_headers))
  │     The tool marks each file it hands out, so the browser
  │     asks fresh next time instead of showing an old copy.
  │     This is why a changed map shows up on a plain reload.
  │     The tool also writes on each text file the time it last
  │     changed. When the file did not change since the copy the
  │     browser holds, the tool answers "not changed" and sends
  │     no file, so the browser shows its own copy at once.
  │
  ●  the tool stands at the door until you stop it
        Ask after ask, it answers. Ctrl-c closes the door.
        Only a writing, a compile, a new file, or a new human file changes the project; every
        other knock reads and leaves it as it is.
        The page can ask if a newer human is ready. When you
        tell it to update, the tool [waits](idle) until no
        knock is writing and no writing waits in the queue of
        any project, then closes the door and starts again as
        the newer human.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  when the answer is not a file                         ([the answer](send_json))
     The fresh map, all the maps in one, the queue of waiting
     writings, and the word back from a writing, a new file,
     or a new human file are not files on disk. The tool
     writes them out as one block of JSON with its length in
     front.
     An answer longer than 1024 bytes goes packed small when
     the browser can unpack it.
     The fresh map also carries a mark made from its words.
     When the browser shows the same mark, the map did not
     change: the tool answers "not changed" and sends no map.
     The fresh map also tells, for each map and human file,
     [the time it last changed](map_stamps), so the page sees
     which map changed.
     To list the files of the fresh map, the tool keeps what
     it found in each folder and looks again only in a folder
     that changed, so a reload stays quick in a big project.

  when you want to see the asks                           ([the mute](log_message))
     human serve --log writes one line per knock.
     Without it the tool stays silent, because one page load
     is many knocks and they would flood your screen.

  when a second project wants a door
     The first serve holds door 8010. Type human serve in the
     second project too: it [gives the project](hand_over) to
     the first server and prints its own address, with its own
     id. A project is given only from this machine; a knock
     from another machine that gives a project is refused.
     You can still give a project its own door: human serve
     --port 8011, and read it at
     http://localhost:8011/<id>/human/web.html.
